title: Demand
description: Class 11 Economics: meaning of demand, demand schedule and demand curve, the law of demand and its exceptions, determinants of demand, and movement along vs shift in the demand curve.

topics.title: Demand, Demand Schedule, Curve and the Law of Demand
topics.concept:
In economics, demand means the quantity of a good that a consumer is willing and able to buy at a given price during a given period of time. Mere desire is not demand — it must be backed by the ability to pay (money) and the willingness to spend it. Individual demand is the demand of a single consumer; market demand is the total demand of all consumers in the market.

A demand schedule is a table showing the quantities demanded at different prices. When these are plotted on a graph (price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis), we get the demand curve, which slopes downward from left to right:

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is mere desire for a good not 'demand' in economics?
examples.solution:
Demand needs more than a wish.

  • Desire must be backed by the ability to pay and the willingness to spend.
  • Without these, it is only a want, not demand.
examples.answer: Because demand must be backed by the ability to pay and the willingness to buy at a given price — desire alone is not demand.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the difference between individual and market demand?
examples.solution:
One vs all.

  • Individual demand is the demand of a single consumer.
  • Market demand is the total demand of all consumers.
examples.answer: Individual demand is one consumer's demand; market demand is the total demand of all consumers in the market.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why does the demand curve slope downward?
examples.solution:
Price and quantity move oppositely.

  • As price falls, quantity demanded rises (and vice versa).
  • This inverse relation gives a downward-sloping curve.
examples.answer: Because price and quantity demanded are inversely related — as price falls, quantity demanded rises — giving a downward slope.

recap:
• Demand = quantity a consumer is willing and able to buy at a given price in a period (desire + ability + willingness).
  • Individual vs market demand (all consumers).
  • Demand schedule (table) → demand curve (downward sloping: price ↓ → quantity ↑).

quiz.q: Demand in economics must be backed by:
quiz.explanation: Demand = desire + ability to pay + willingness to spend.
Price and quantity demanded are inversely related, so the curve slopes downward.

topics.title: The Law of Demand and Its Determinants
topics.concept:
The relationship just described is summed up in the Law of Demand: other things remaining constant, as the price of a good falls, its quantity demanded rises, and as the price rises, its quantity demanded falls. Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions. The phrase "other things remaining constant" (ceteris paribus) is crucial — the law holds only if the other factors that affect demand do not change.

What are those other determinants of demand? Besides the price of the good itself, demand depends on:

  • Income of the consumer — usually, higher income raises demand (for normal goods).
  • Prices of related goods — for substitutes (tea and coffee) a rise in one's price raises demand for the other; for complements (car and petrol) a rise in one's price lowers demand for the other.
  • Tastes and preferences — fashion, advertising and habits.
  • Expectations — if prices are expected to rise, people buy more now.
  • Size and composition of population — more buyers raise market demand.

The law of demand applies to most goods, but there are a few exceptions where more is bought even at higher prices: Giffen goods (very inferior necessities like a cheap staple food), goods of status/prestige (like diamonds, bought to show off — Veblen goods), cases of expected future price changes, and ignorance where people judge quality by price. In these special cases the demand curve may slope upward.

examples.solution:
Inverse relation, other things constant.

  • Other things remaining constant, as price falls quantity demanded rises, and as price rises quantity demanded falls.
examples.answer: Other things being equal, the quantity demanded of a good rises when its price falls and falls when its price rises.

examples.problem: Example 2: Tea and coffee are substitutes. If the price of tea rises, what happens to the demand for coffee?
examples.solution:
Substitutes move together in demand.

  • People switch from costlier tea to coffee.
  • So the demand for coffee rises.
examples.answer: The demand for coffee rises (consumers switch from the dearer tea to its substitute).

examples.problem: Example 3: Give one exception to the law of demand.
examples.solution:
Some goods defy the law.

  • Status/prestige goods (e.g. diamonds) — bought more at higher prices to show wealth.
  • (Also Giffen goods, expected price changes, ignorance.)
examples.answer: Status/prestige goods like diamonds (bought more at higher prices); also Giffen goods, expected price changes and ignorance.

recap:
• Law of Demand: ceteris paribus, price ↓ → quantity demanded ↑ (and vice versa) — inverse relation.
  • Determinants: own price, income, prices of related goods (substitutes/complements), tastes, expectations, population.
  • Exceptions: Giffen goods, status/prestige (Veblen) goods, expected price changes, ignorance.

quiz.q: According to the law of demand, when price rises, quantity demanded:
quiz.explanation: Price and quantity demanded are inversely related.

quiz.q: A rise in the price of petrol lowers the demand for cars. Cars and petrol are:
quiz.explanation: Goods used together (car and petrol) are complements.

topics.title: Movement Along vs Shift in the Demand Curve
topics.concept:
It is vital to distinguish two different ways demand can change, because students often confuse them.

Movement along the demand curve happens when the price of the good itself changes, while everything else stays the same. We simply slide from one point to another on the same curve:

  • A fall in price → a movement downward along the curve → more quantity demanded. This is called an extension (or expansion) of demand.
  • A rise in price → a movement upward along the curve → less quantity demanded. This is called a contraction of demand.

Shift in the demand curve happens when a factor other than the price of the good changes (income, prices of related goods, tastes, etc.). The whole curve moves to a new position:

  • If more is demanded at the same price (e.g. income rises) → the curve shifts to the right — an increase in demand.
  • If less is demanded at the same price → the curve shifts to the left — a decrease in demand.

The simple rule: a change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve; a change in any other determinant causes a shift of the curve. Keeping this distinction clear is one of the most important skills in microeconomics.

examples.problem: Example 1: A fall in the price of a good leads to which change — movement or shift?
examples.solution:
Own price changed.

  • A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve.
  • A price fall is a downward movement (extension of demand).
examples.answer: A movement along the curve (an extension/expansion of demand).

examples.problem: Example 2: A rise in consumer income makes people buy more at the same price. What happens to the demand curve?
examples.solution:
A non-price factor changed.

  • More is demanded at the same price.
  • The whole curve shifts to the right (increase in demand).
examples.answer: The demand curve shifts to the right (an increase in demand).

examples.problem: Example 3: State the simple rule distinguishing a movement from a shift.
examples.solution:
It is about what changed.

  • Change in own price → movement along the curve.
  • Change in any other determinant → shift of the curve.
examples.answer: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve; a change in any other determinant causes a shift of the curve.

recap:
• Movement along the curve = change in the good's own price: price↓ = extension (down), price↑ = contraction (up).
  • Shift of the curve = change in other determinants (income, related prices, tastes): right = increase, left = decrease in demand.
  • Rule: own price → movement; other factor → shift.

quiz.explanation: Own-price changes cause movement along the same curve.

quiz.q: A rightward shift of the demand curve means demand has:
quiz.explanation: A rightward shift = more demanded at each price = increase in demand.

questions.q: Demand for a good must be backed by:
questions.explanation: Demand needs desire plus ability and willingness to pay.

questions.q: The total demand of all consumers in a market is:
questions.explanation: The sum of all consumers' demand is market demand.

questions.q: A table showing quantity demanded at different prices is a:
questions.explanation: That table is the demand schedule.

questions.q: The demand curve normally slopes:
questions.explanation: Price and quantity demanded are inversely related.

questions.q: The law of demand holds 'other things remaining':
questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus — other things remaining constant.

questions.q: When price rises, quantity demanded usually:
questions.explanation: Higher price reduces quantity demanded.

questions.q: Tea and coffee are examples of:
questions.explanation: Goods that replace each other are substitutes.

questions.q: Car and petrol are examples of:
questions.explanation: Goods used together are complements.

questions.q: Which is a determinant of demand other than the good's own price?
options: The day of the week only
questions.explanation: Income is a key determinant of demand.

questions.q: An exception to the law of demand is a:
questions.explanation: Giffen goods are a classic exception to the law of demand.

questions.q: A change in the good's own price causes a:
questions.explanation: Own-price changes move us along the same curve.

questions.q: A fall in price causing more to be demanded is called:
questions.explanation: A downward movement due to a price fall is an extension of demand.

questions.q: A change in income or tastes causes a:
questions.explanation: Non-price determinants shift the whole curve.

questions.q: A rightward shift of the demand curve indicates:
questions.explanation: Right shift = more demanded at each price = increase.

questions.q: More demanded at a higher price would be shown by:
questions.explanation: Exceptions to the law give an upward-sloping demand curve.

questions.q: A poor person wants a car but cannot afford one. In economic terms this is:
options: A want, not demand (no ability to pay)
questions.explanation: Without the ability to pay, the desire is only a want — not demand.

questions.q: The price of sugar falls and households buy more sugar. This is best described as a:
questions.explanation: Because the good's own price changed, we slide down the same curve — an extension of demand.

questions.q: People's incomes rise and they buy more clothes at every price. The clothes demand curve will:
questions.explanation: A rise in income (a non-price factor) raises demand at each price, shifting the curve right.

questions.q: When the price of coffee rises, the demand for tea increases. This happens because the two goods are:
questions.explanation: Consumers switch from dearer coffee to its substitute, tea, raising tea's demand.

questions.q: Expecting petrol prices to rise next week, drivers fill their tanks today. This shows demand is affected by:
questions.explanation: Expected future price rises increase present demand — an expectations effect.

questions.q: A diamond necklace sells more when its price is raised because owning it signals wealth. This is an exception known as a:
questions.explanation: Prestige goods bought to display wealth can have demand rising with price — a Veblen-good exception.

questions.q: A leftward shift of the demand curve for a good could be caused by:
options: A fall in consumer income (for a normal good)
A fall in the good's own price
A rise in the good's own price
questions.explanation: Lower income reduces demand at every price, shifting the curve left (own-price changes only move along it).

questions.q: Why is the phrase 'other things remaining constant' essential to the law of demand?
options: Because if other determinants also change, the simple inverse price–quantity relation may not hold
questions.explanation: The law isolates the effect of price alone; if income, tastes, etc. also move, the observed relation can differ.

questions.q: A rise in a good's own price causing less to be bought is shown as:
options: An upward movement (contraction) along the curve
questions.explanation: Higher own price means we slide up the same curve — a contraction of demand.

questions.q: Which single rule correctly separates a movement from a shift?
options: Own price → movement; any other factor → shift
questions.explanation: Own-price changes move us along the curve; changes in other determinants shift the whole curve.
